A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same U-Cast research. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–C are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original U-Cast forecasting results, computational measurements, ablations, and appendix analyses, including Table 1 and Figures 4–15.

after.justification: v2 retains the original forecasting experiments and appendix analyses and reports revised inference timings and additional computational findings in Appendix C.2.

M1.justification: The U-Net architecture, MAE-to-CRPS curriculum, MC Dropout, Muon optimization, and deep ensembling remain unchanged. Compilation is newly documented implementation information; full-state prediction is proposed only as future work.

E1.justification: Both versions retain ERA5 training on 1979–2019, WeatherBench 2 evaluations on 2020 and 2022, the same atmospheric variables, and the existing 1° computational experiment. No dataset, forecasting task, or environmental test scenario is added.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds MOSAIC to the computational comparison, reporting 16 H100-days of training and approximately 3 seconds per rollout. Appendix C.2 explains the literature-based latency estimate. Forecast-accuracy comparator membership remains unchanged.

E3.justification: Table 2 changes U-Cast's reported timing hardware from H200/A100 to H100/A100. v2 also adds one-versus-ten-member timing comparisons and a MOSAIC latency extrapolation protocol. The 60-step timing workload and existing forecasting evaluation settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 4.3 and Appendix C.2 add limited efficiency analyses examining ensemble batching and compilation benefits. Existing optimizer, dropout, curriculum, ensemble-size, generalization, spectral, and qualitative analyses are retained; the added spectral explanation is not a new experiment.

E5.justification: Appendix C.2 newly specifies timing averages over repeated rollouts, describing six rollouts with the first discarded for compilation and startup overhead. v1 gives no corresponding repetition information. This disclosure does not establish an increase in runs; no forecast confidence intervals or significance tests are added.

E6.justification: Changes are concentrated in computational results. Table 2 replaces 1.5° U-Cast timings of 11/17 seconds on H200/A100 with 2/3.6 seconds on H100/A100; 1° timings change from 12/19 to 3/5.2 seconds. v2 adds MOSAIC costs, a 12-second ten-member rollout, and a reported compilation benefit near 50%. These are revised or newly reported measurements, not an established identical-setting speedup. Forecast-accuracy and existing ablation results remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The loss definitions in Equations 1–5 and metric definitions in Appendix B, Equations 6–7, are unchanged. No formal assumptions, proofs, or substantive mathematical derivations are added or revised.

C1.justification: The central claims about simple architectures, competitive forecasting skill, and inexpensive probabilistic training remain. The quantitative efficiency headline changes: the introduction replaces an 11-second single 60-step forecast with 2 seconds, while the abstract replaces a 60-step ensemble forecast in 11 seconds with a 15-day ensemble forecast in 3 seconds.

C2.justification: Appendix C.7 newly connects spectral artifacts to residual prediction training and suggests full-state prediction as a possible remedy. Section 6 states long-rollout instability more definitively while weakening its proposed explanation from 'likely stems' to 'might stem' from absent autoregressive training.

D1.justification: Appendix C.2 newly documents mixed precision, torch.compile, and timing coverage including denormalization, autoregressive input updates, and CPU transfers. Appendix C.4 clarifies that all reported metrics use 50-member ensembles. The reported architecture implementation length changes from under 500 to under 300 lines; code-access information remains unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds Zhdanov et al. and positions MOSAIC as an efficient concurrent probabilistic forecaster, also citing it in the spectral-artifact discussion. It softens the characterization of prior convolutional work. ArchesWeatherGen and AIFS-CRPS publication updates refer to retained works rather than additional comparators.

P1.justification: There are localized rewrites in the introduction, related work, discussion, and limitations; reordered contribution bullets; a separate concurrent-work paragraph; and updated conference publication text. The overall narrative and section organization remain stable.

P2.justification: Table 2 gains a MOSAIC row. Figures 1 and 6 are redrawn to reflect revised latency values, including changed plotting ranges or bubble legends. Figure 4 moves between columns, with accompanying text reflow. The other scientific displays retain their content.

improvement.justification: v2 modestly improves reproducibility and context: Appendix C.2 explains previously unspecified timing procedures, Table 2 includes an efficient concurrent comparator with explicit estimation assumptions, and the limitations discussion becomes more informative. These benefits support a limited quality improvement without changing the forecasting contribution. The abstract's ensemble runtime remains underspecified, and MOSAIC's latency comparison relies on extrapolation, limiting the strength of the efficiency conclusions.
